meta.title: Who originally recorded "Seven Bridges Road"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not an Eagles original. Steve Young wrote and first recorded “Seven Bridges Road” in 1969 for his A&M debut; Eagles cut it live in 1980.
meta.ogDescription: Steve Young wrote it and recorded it first, in 1969 on A&M. Eagles’ famous harmony version is a live cover from July 1980.

answer.label: Not an Eagles original — a 1969 Steve Young album track on A&M
answer.sourceLine: The five-part harmony most people picture is Eagles, recorded live in July 1980 and issued as a single that December — and it is very widely assumed to be an Eagles original. It is not. “Seven Bridges Road” was written by Steve Young and first recorded by him in 1969 for his A&M debut Rock Salt & Nails, where it was nearly left off entirely: producer Tommy LiPuma did not want Young cutting his own material, and guitarist James Burton talked him into recording it. Young’s original was an album track that did not chart, and the song reached the public through a chain of covers before Eagles ever put it on tape.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: A&M
original.released: An album track on Steve Young’s debut LP Rock Salt & Nails, issued by A&M Records in November 1969 (catalogue SP 4177), recorded at A&M Studios in Hollywood with Tommy LiPuma producing.
original.charted: Did not chart. It was the seventh track on a debut album that sold poorly; a Hollywood publisher had already told Young the song “wasn’t commercial enough.”
original.cover: Eagles recorded it live at the Santa Monica Civic Auditorium on 28 July 1980 for Eagles Live, and Asylum issued it as a single on 15 December 1980. It reached No. 21 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 55 on the country chart — the band’s last Top 40 hit until the 1994 reunion.
trail: 1969 — Steve Young records it for Rock Salt & Nails ↗, his A&M debut, backed by James Burton, Hal Blaine, Gram Parsons and Gene Clark.

1973 — Iain Matthews builds the close-harmony arrangement on his August 1973 album Valley Hi, produced by Michael Nesmith, who sang on it. This, not Young’s record, is the version Eagles heard — see the song’s history ↗.
1980 — Eagles’ live version, taped 28 July at the Santa Monica Civic Auditorium, appears on Eagles Live ↗ and as an Asylum single, peaking at No. 21.
2000 — Ricochet’s country revival, its video filmed on the real Woodley Road in Montgomery, Alabama, reaches No. 48 on the country chart.

authors.name: Steve Young
authors.kicker: The original recording artist — and the writer
authors.heading: Steve Young
authors.bio: Young was a Georgia-born singer-songwriter whose 1969 A&M debut Rock Salt & Nails is now treated as a foundational country-rock record, cut with James Burton, Hal Blaine, Gram Parsons and Gene Clark in the room. He wrote “Seven Bridges Road” about Woodley Road south of Montgomery, Alabama — a two-lane road with seven bridges that he and his friends drove at night — and said he never quite understood why it travelled so far. He also wrote “Lonesome, On’ry and Mean,” recorded by Waylon Jennings, and “Montgomery in the Rain,” recorded by Hank Williams Jr. He died in Nashville in 2016.

authors.name: Eagles
authors.heading: Eagles
authors.metaLine: Formed 1971, Los Angeles · American rock band
authors.bio: Eagles used the song as a warm-up in stadium locker rooms and then as a concert opener, five voices around a single microphone, long before they recorded it. Their version was captured at the Santa Monica Civic Auditorium on 28 July 1980, days before the band broke up, and Asylum released it as a single that December; it went to No. 21 and became their final Top 40 hit until 1994. The performance is genuinely, thrillingly theirs — the only error in the popular story is chronological.

misattribution.heading: Right band, wrong origin
misattribution.intro: The Eagles record is a live cover of a song that had already been circulating for over a decade under other names.

items.why: Their harmony version, from Eagles Live, is so identified with the band that it is routinely listed among their originals.
Recorded for Rock Salt & Nails and released by A&M in November 1969 — a solo country-folk performance with no group harmony at all.
Young is credited as sole writer on every release of the song, the Eagles single included.
The stacked close-harmony treatment came from Matthews’ Valley Hi, produced by Michael Nesmith, who later said the Eagles took the vocal arrangement note for note.

misattribution.truthLine: Written and first recorded by Steve Young in 1969; the harmony everyone hums is a 1973 Iain Matthews idea that Eagles carried onto a 1980 live stage.

context.heading: Why the cover swallowed the original
lead: Young’s 1969 record is a solitary thing — one voice, one guitar, a road in Alabama at night. It was almost not recorded at all: producer Tommy LiPuma had signed Young to be an interpreter of folk and country standards, not a writer, and it took James Burton pushing back in the studio to get the song onto tape. A Hollywood publisher had already passed on it as insufficiently commercial. The album sold accordingly.

What changed the song’s fate was not Eagles but Iain Matthews. His 1973 Valley Hi version, produced by Michael Nesmith at Nesmith’s Countryside Ranch studio, replaced the lone voice with layered close harmony. Don Henley owned a copy of that album, and the two camps overlapped at the Troubadour. Nesmith’s later verdict was blunt: the Eagles lifted the vocal arrangement note for note, and he would rather they stole it from him than from anybody else. Once five Eagles sang it into one microphone to open a stadium show, the earlier records had no chance of being the one people remembered.
detailsBody: Early 1960s: Young, living on and off in Montgomery, Alabama, begins writing about Woodley Road and its seven wooden bridges.
1969: The song is cut, over the producer’s objection, at A&M Studios in Hollywood during the Rock Salt & Nails sessions.
November 1969: A&M releases the album (SP 4177). “Seven Bridges Road” is track seven and does not chart.
1973: Iain Matthews records the close-harmony arrangement for Valley Hi, produced by Michael Nesmith.
28 July 1980: Eagles perform it at the Santa Monica Civic Auditorium; the tape becomes part of Eagles Live.
15 December 1980: Asylum issues the Eagles single. It peaks at No. 21 pop and No. 55 country.
Young himself re-recorded the song three more times — for Reprise in 1972, RCA Victor in 1978 and Rounder in 1981 — so not every “Steve Young” version in circulation is the original.

A note on the paperwork: Wikipedia’s song infobox also lists a Steve Young 45 on Reprise backed with “Many Rivers,” but its dating sits oddly against the A&M album. The documented first recording is the November 1969 A&M album track.
context.pull: A song about one road in Alabama, rebuilt twice before the world heard it.
